set1.q: A 74-year-old woman is in cardiac arrest. Which finding defines ventricular standstill?
opts: QRS complexes with no P waves
QRS complexes without P waves describe a ventricular rhythm such as ventricular tachycardia. Standstill has P waves and no QRS.
P waves with no QRS complexes
Correct. In ventricular standstill there are atrial contractions but no ventricular contractions: obvious upright P waves march out with no QRS.
A flat line with no waves
A flat line is asystole. Ventricular standstill keeps its P waves.
Chaotic waves with no QRS
Chaotic waves without measurable complexes are ventricular fibrillation. Standstill has orderly P waves.

set1.q: A 70-year-old man's PR intervals just before and just after a dropped beat are the same duration. Which block is this?
opts: Second-degree type I
Type I shows PR intervals of different duration around the dropped beat: longest before it, reset after it.
Second-degree type II
Correct. If the PR intervals before and after the dropped beat are equal in duration, it is always second-degree type II.
Third-degree block
Third-degree block has no PR relationship at all; the P waves are unrelated to the QRS complexes.
First-degree block
First-degree block conducts every P wave and never drops a beat, so there is no dropped beat to measure around.

set1.q: A 74-year-old man in cardiac arrest has this rhythm. Which finding on the strip defines it?
opts: Identical wide QRS complexes
Identical wide complexes are monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Here there is no repeating complex to measure.
No measurable P, QRS or T waves
Correct. In ventricular fibrillation there are no measurable P waves, QRS complexes or T waves, only chaotic irregular activity.
P waves with no QRS complexes
Upright P waves without QRS complexes are ventricular standstill. There are no P waves on this strip.
A completely flat baseline
A flat line is asystole. This baseline is never still: it is continuous chaotic electrical activity.

set1.q: A 65-year-old man has more P waves than QRS complexes, and his PR interval changes at random from beat to beat. Which block is this?
opts: Second-degree type I
Type I PR intervals are not random: they lengthen progressively in each group until a P wave is not conducted.
Second-degree type II
Type II has a constant PR interval on every conducted beat, with some P waves not conducted.
First-degree block
First-degree block has one QRS for every P wave and a long but consistent PR interval.
Third-degree block
Correct. P waves unrelated to the QRS, so that no PR interval repeats, is third-degree block: the atria and ventricles beat independently.

set1.q: A 68-year-old man with chest pain develops complete heart block. Which infarct location is especially associated with it?
opts: Inferior
Correct. Acute myocardial infarction, especially inferior infarction, is one of the most common causes of third-degree block.
Anterior
Anterior infarction is not the location singled out. Complete heart block is especially associated with inferior infarction.
Lateral
Lateral infarction is not the classic association. Third-degree block is especially linked to inferior infarction.
Septal
Septal infarction is not the classic association. Inferior infarction is the one especially linked to complete block.

set1.q: A 71-year-old man in cardiac arrest has pulseless electrical activity. Which statement about its appearance is correct?
opts: It always has wide QRS complexes
Pulseless electrical activity can look like any organized rhythm, including one with a narrow QRS.
It shows no electrical activity
No electrical activity is asystole. Pulseless electrical activity has organized electrical activity on the monitor.
It can look like any organized rhythm
Correct. Pulseless electrical activity can look like any organized rhythm, even normal sinus; the strip alone cannot make the diagnosis.
It shows P waves but no QRS
P waves without QRS complexes are ventricular standstill. Pulseless electrical activity can be any organized rhythm.

set1.q: A 74-year-old man has second-degree type II block. Where is the block usually located?
opts: High in the atrioventricular node
A block within the atrioventricular node itself is second-degree type I (Wenckebach). Type II sits lower.
In the sinoatrial node
The sinoatrial node keeps firing in type II; its P waves march out. The block is below the atrioventricular node.
In the atrial muscle
Atrial conduction is intact; the P waves are normal. The block is below the atrioventricular node.
Below the atrioventricular node
Correct. Type II is an infranodal block, low in the conduction system at the His bundle, generally in the His-Purkinje system.

set1.q: A 52-year-old woman is being evaluated for a conduction delay. Which hallmark defines first-degree block?
opts: A PR that lengthens until a beat drops
Progressive PR lengthening with a dropped beat is second-degree type I. First-degree block has no dropped beats.
Sinus rhythm with a PR beyond 0.2 seconds
Correct. The hallmark of first-degree block is a sinus rhythm having a PR interval beyond 0.2 seconds in duration.
A constant PR with some dropped beats
A constant PR with dropped QRS complexes is second-degree type II. First-degree block drops nothing.
P waves unrelated to the QRS complexes
P waves unrelated to the QRS complexes are third-degree block. In first-degree block each P wave is married to its QRS.

set1.q: A 78-year-old woman's third-degree block has narrow QRS complexes on this strip. Where is her ventricular escape most likely coming from?
opts: The Purkinje and bundle-branch fibers
An escape from the Purkinje or bundle-branch fibers spreads outside the normal pathway and is wide. These complexes are narrow.
The sinoatrial node
The sinoatrial node drives only the atria in complete block. Its impulses never reach the ventricles.
The atrioventricular junction
Correct. In third-degree block the QRS is narrow or wide depending on the origin; a narrow escape comes from the atrioventricular junction, above the bundle branches.
Many ventricular foci
Many foci firing at once is ventricular fibrillation. A complete block has one regular escape rhythm.

set1.q: A 77-year-old man is pulseless. His monitor shows this. What is the rhythm?
opts: Ventricular standstill
Correct. Obvious upright P waves march across the strip with no QRS complexes: the atria contract but the ventricles do not, with no pulse.
Asystole
Asystole is a flat line with no electrical activity. This strip has regular P waves, so the atria are still firing.
Third-degree atrioventricular block
Third-degree block keeps a slow escape QRS beating independently of the P waves. Here there are no QRS complexes at all.
Pulseless electrical activity
Pulseless electrical activity is an organized rhythm with QRS complexes but no pulse. This strip has no QRS complexes.

set1.q: A 68-year-old man's monitor shows polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Which rate and regularity fit it?
opts: 300 to 500 per minute, irregular
That is ventricular fibrillation, which has no measurable QRS. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia runs at 100 to 300 per minute.
100 to 300 per minute, regular
A regular ventricular tachycardia is the monomorphic form. The polymorphic form is irregular.
100 to 300 per minute, irregular
Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is an irregular ventricular tachycardia at 100 to 300 per minute.
20 to 40 per minute, regular
That is the rate of a ventricular escape rhythm. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is a fast rhythm at 100 to 300 per minute.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man has this strip. What does the PR interval do across each group of beats?
opts: It stays constant, then a beat drops
A constant PR before a dropped beat is second-degree type II. Here the PR grows with each beat.
It varies at random
A PR that varies with no pattern is third-degree block. This PR changes in a predictable, progressive way.
It is long but never changes
A long, unchanging PR with no dropped beats is first-degree block. This strip drops a beat after the PR grows.
It lengthens until a beat drops
Correct. In Wenckebach the PR interval prolongs progressively until a P wave is not conducted; the dropped QRS resets the cycle.

set1.q: A 67-year-old man has Wenckebach block in his atrioventricular node. What happens to conduction through the node from beat to beat?
opts: It stays fixed, then fails suddenly
A constant PR with sudden dropped beats is second-degree type II, a block below the node; in Wenckebach the nodal delay grows beat by beat.
It speeds up until a beat drops
Nothing in Wenckebach speeds conduction; the PR interval lengthens with each beat before the dropped QRS.
It slows until one impulse fails
Correct. Conduction through the atrioventricular node slows a little more with each beat, so the PR lengthens, until one impulse is not conducted and a QRS drops; then the cycle starts over.
It fails completely on every beat
Complete failure of conduction is third-degree block, with P waves and QRS complexes unrelated; in Wenckebach most impulses are conducted.

set1.q: A 58-year-old woman is unresponsive, and her monitor shows this organized rhythm. Which finding would make it pulseless electrical activity?
opts: Absent P waves
This rhythm has a P wave before each QRS, and pulseless electrical activity can look like any organized rhythm. The pulse decides it.
An irregular rhythm
Regularity does not define it; pulseless electrical activity can be any organized rhythm. Only the missing pulse does.
Inverted T waves
T wave direction does not make the diagnosis. Organized electrical activity becomes pulseless electrical activity when there is no pulse.
No palpable pulse
Correct. Pulseless electrical activity can look like any organized rhythm, even normal sinus; it is the absence of a pulse that makes the diagnosis.

set1.q: A 60-year-old woman's strip shows a dropped beat. How does the PR interval after the dropped beat compare with the one before it?
opts: It is the same
Equal PR intervals before and after the dropped beat would make this second-degree type II. Here the PR resets shorter.
It is longer
The PR is longest just before the dropped beat. After the drop it resets to its shortest.
It cannot be measured
The P wave after the dropped beat is conducted, so its PR can be measured; it is shorter than the one before the drop.
It is shorter
Correct. After the dropped beat the cycle begins over, so the next PR is shorter than the last, longest PR before the drop: second-degree type I.

set1.q: An 80-year-old man has this paced strip. Why are the QRS complexes wide?
opts: The atrioventricular node is blocked
The width does not come from a nodal block. It comes from the beat starting in the ventricle, where the pacemaker lead fires.
The ventricles are paced below the atria
Correct. Ventricular pacemakers pace the ventricles below the level of the atria, so the impulse spreads outside the normal pathway and the QRS is wide.
Many ventricular foci fire at once
Chaotic firing of many foci is ventricular fibrillation. Here one paced focus fires on schedule after each spike.
The atria are being paced
Atrial pacing gives a normal, narrow QRS through the normal pathway. A wide QRS after a spike means the ventricle is paced.

set1.q: A 52-year-old woman had this rhythm and was resuscitated. Which finding on her earlier electrocardiogram would best explain it?
opts: A prolonged PR interval
A PR interval beyond 0.2 seconds is first-degree block, a benign delay in the atrioventricular node that does not lead to torsades.
Grouped beating with dropped beats
Grouped beating is second-degree type I block, a conduction problem in the atrioventricular node, not the setup for torsades.
A pacer spike before each P wave
A spike before each P wave is an atrial pacemaker working normally. It does not explain a twisting ventricular tachycardia.
A prolonged QT interval
Correct. The rhythm is torsades de pointes, and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia of this kind is usually a consequence of a prolonged QT interval.

set1.q: A 71-year-old man has second-degree type II block. Compared with type I, how is type II characterized?
opts: Less common but more serious
Correct. Second-degree type II is less common but more serious than type I, and it is always a sign of underlying conduction system disease.
More common and more benign
Type II is the rarer and more dangerous of the two second-degree blocks.
More common and more serious
Type II is more serious, but it is the less common of the two second-degree blocks.
Less common and more benign
Type II is less common, but it is not benign: it is always a sign of disease of the conduction system.

set1.q: A 61-year-old man is found unresponsive and pulseless. His monitor shows this. What is the rhythm?
opts: Asystole
Asystole is a lack of electrical activity, a flat line. This strip shows continuous small chaotic waves, which is fibrillation.
Pulseless electrical activity
Pulseless electrical activity is an organized rhythm without a pulse. These waves are disorganized, with no QRS complexes.
Fine ventricular fibrillation
Correct. Low-amplitude chaotic waves with no measurable P waves, QRS complexes or T waves are fine ventricular fibrillation, not a flat line.
Ventricular standstill
Ventricular standstill shows upright P waves marching across with no QRS. This strip has no P waves, only chaotic ventricular activity.

set1.q: A 75-year-old man has third-degree atrioventricular block. How do his atrial and ventricular rates compare?
opts: The ventricular rate is faster
The ventricles are driven by a slower escape pacemaker below the block, so they beat slower than the atria.
The atrial rate is faster
Correct. In third-degree block the atrial rate is faster than the ventricular rate, which depends on a slower escape pacemaker.
The two rates are equal
Equal rates with every P wave conducted would not be complete block. The atria outpace the ventricles.
There is no atrial rate
The atria keep beating normally under the sinoatrial node; their P waves march through the strip.

set1.q: A 79-year-old woman with a pacemaker has this strip. Which pacing does it show?
opts: Atrial pacing
Atrial pacing has one spike before the P wave and a normal, narrow QRS. These QRS complexes are wide and carry their own spike.
Ventricular pacing
Ventricular pacing has a spike before each QRS only. This strip also has a spike before each P wave.
Ventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia has no pacer spikes. Here two spikes start every cycle.
Atrial and ventricular pacing
Correct. A spike precedes each P wave and another precedes every wide QRS: both chambers are being paced, which is rare.

set1.q: A 70-year-old man's monitor shows regular, wide complexes with no P waves. Which rate range defines this rhythm?
opts: 300 to 500 per minute
That is the rate of ventricular fibrillation, which is irregular and has no measurable QRS. Ventricular tachycardia runs at 100 to 300.
100 to 300 per minute
Correct. Ventricular tachycardia runs at 100 to 300 per minute, regular, with wide QRS complexes and no P waves.
20 to 40 per minute
A ventricular rate of 20 to 40 belongs to a slow escape rhythm, not a tachycardia. Ventricular tachycardia runs at 100 to 300 per minute.
60 to 100 per minute
That is a normal rate. Ventricular tachycardia is, by name, a tachycardia, at 100 to 300 per minute.

set1.q: A 57-year-old man known to have a prolonged QT interval becomes unresponsive. His monitor shows this. What is the rhythm?
opts: Torsades de pointes
Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia twisting around the baseline, in a patient with a prolonged QT interval, is torsades de pointes.
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
The monomorphic form keeps one complex shape and a regular rhythm. Here the shape and amplitude keep changing.
Fine ventricular fibrillation
Fine ventricular fibrillation is low-amplitude chaotic squiggles with no measurable complexes. These complexes are large and wide.
Asystole
Asystole is a flat line with no electrical activity. This strip shows continuous, rapid ventricular activity.

set1.q: A 41-year-old man has this strip, and his rhythm looks like sinus at first glance. Which single measurement makes the diagnosis?
opts: The QRS duration
The QRS can be narrow or wide in first-degree block, so it does not make the diagnosis. The PR interval does.
The PR interval
Correct. This is first-degree block, and the PR interval is all that diagnoses it: a sinus rhythm with a PR beyond 0.2 seconds.
The P-P interval
The P waves are regular, as in any sinus rhythm. That says nothing about conduction through the atrioventricular node.
The heart rate
The rate is slow or normal in first-degree block, so rate cannot make the diagnosis. The PR interval does.

set1.q: A 75-year-old man with a history of conduction disease has this strip. What is the rhythm?
opts: Second-degree type II (Mobitz II)
Correct. A constant PR on the conducted beats with dropped QRS complexes, here with wide QRS complexes, is second-degree type II.
Second-degree type I (Wenckebach)
Wenckebach shows progressive PR lengthening before the drop. These PR intervals do not change.
Third-degree (complete) block
Third-degree block has P waves unrelated to the QRS. Here each conducted P wave has the same PR before its QRS.
Ventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia is a fast, regular wide-complex rhythm with no P waves. This rhythm is slow, with P waves and dropped beats.

set1.q: A 59-year-old man's monitor shows this wide-complex rhythm. Which feature marks it as monomorphic?
opts: Every complex has the same shape
Correct. Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia is regular, with complexes of one identical shape; the polymorphic form is irregular and changes shape.
The rate is above 100 per minute
Both monomorphic and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia run at 100 to 300 per minute, so the rate cannot separate them.
The QRS complexes are wide
Every ventricular tachycardia is wide because it starts in the ventricles. Width says ventricular, not which form.
No P waves are visible
P waves are typically absent in both forms. What separates monomorphic from polymorphic is whether the complexes keep one shape.

set1.q: A 72-year-old man in cardiac arrest has this rhythm. Which finding separates it from ventricular tachycardia?
opts: No organized QRS complexes
Correct. This is ventricular fibrillation: chaotic waves with no measurable QRS. Ventricular tachycardia has organized, identical wide complexes.
Absence of P waves
Neither rhythm shows P waves married to a QRS, so their absence does not separate the two.
A ventricular origin
Both rhythms come from the ventricles. The difference is a single organized focus versus chaotic firing of many foci.
A fast rate
Both are fast: 100 to 300 per minute for tachycardia, 300 to 500 for fibrillation. Organization is what separates them.

set1.q: A 77-year-old woman with a ventricular pacemaker has a T wave after each paced beat. In which direction does that T wave point?
opts: The same direction as the QRS
A T wave in the same direction as the QRS is the normal pattern of a conducted beat, not a paced ventricle.
Hidden inside the QRS
The T wave of a paced beat is separate and visible after the wide QRS, pointing the opposite way.
Opposite to the QRS complex
Correct. A ventricular paced beat has a contralateral T wave, one going the opposite direction of the QRS complex.
Absent after every paced beat
Paced ventricular beats repolarize, so a T wave follows each one. It points opposite to the QRS.

set1.q: A 73-year-old man's regular P waves appear to march through his QRS-T complexes. Which block does this describe?
opts: Second-degree type II (Mobitz II)
Type II conducts most P waves with a fixed PR. The P waves are tied to the QRS complexes except for the dropped beats.
First-degree block
First-degree block keeps every P wave married to a QRS, after a long PR.
Third-degree block
Correct. Regular P-P intervals unrelated to regular R-R intervals, with P waves that march through the QRS-T complexes, are the hallmark of third-degree block.
Second-degree type I
Type I P waves are married to the QRS complexes, with a lengthening PR, until one drops.

set1.q: A 64-year-old man has palpitations and a palpable pulse. His monitor shows this rhythm. What is it?
opts: Ventricular tachycardia
Correct. Regular, wide, identical complexes at a fast rate with no P waves are ventricular tachycardia; this example runs at 140 per minute.
Torsades de pointes
Torsades de pointes is polymorphic: the complexes change shape and twist around the baseline. Every complex here has the same shape.
Ventricular fibrillation
Ventricular fibrillation has no measurable QRS complexes, only chaotic waves at 300 to 500 per minute. These complexes are organized and identical.
Ventricular paced rhythm
A ventricular paced rhythm puts a pacer spike before every wide QRS. No spikes precede these complexes, so a ventricular focus is driving them.

opts: Ventricular standstill
Ventricular standstill keeps obvious upright P waves marching across the strip. This tracing has no P waves.
Asystole
Correct. There is no electrical activity, only a wandering baseline: asystole, a lack of electrical activity with no pulse.
Pulseless electrical activity
Pulseless electrical activity is organized electrical activity with no pulse. This tracing has no complexes at all.
Third-degree atrioventricular block

set2.q: An 81-year-old man with a pacemaker has this strip. Which pacing does it show?
opts: Atrial pacing
Atrial pacing is a spike followed by a normal P-QRS-T cycle with a narrow QRS. These complexes are wide.
Atrial and ventricular pacing
Dual pacing shows a spike before the P wave as well as before the QRS. Here the spike comes only before each QRS.
Ventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia has wide complexes but no pacer spikes and a fast rate. Every complex here starts with a spike.
Ventricular pacing
Correct. A pacer spike precedes every wide QRS, and each T wave points opposite to its QRS: the pacemaker is pacing the ventricle.

set2.q: A 76-year-old man with a recent inferior infarction has this strip. What is the rhythm?
opts: Third-degree (complete) block
Correct. The P waves march at their own regular rate and the narrow QRS complexes beat regularly at a slower rate, with no fixed PR: complete heart block.
Second-degree type I (Wenckebach)
Type I PR intervals lengthen in a predictable pattern before a single dropped beat. These PR intervals bear no relation to each other.
Second-degree type II (Mobitz II)
Type II has a constant PR on every conducted beat. Here no two PR intervals are the same.
First-degree atrioventricular block
First-degree block has one QRS per P wave at a long but fixed PR. Here there are more P waves than QRS complexes.

set2.q: A 47-year-old man's PR interval is longer than 0.20 seconds (normal 0.12 to 0.20), and every P wave on this strip is conducted. What does this represent?
opts: A block below the atrioventricular node
A block low in the His bundle is second-degree type II, which drops beats. First-degree block is a delay within the node.
A benign delay in the atrioventricular node
Correct. First-degree block is a benign PR interval delay from slowed conduction through the atrioventricular node; every P wave still gets through.
Complete atrioventricular dissociation
Complete dissociation is third-degree block, where no P waves are conducted. Here every one is.
Intermittent failure to conduct
Intermittent failure, with dropped beats, is second-degree block. First-degree block only slows conduction.

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block Type I, second-degree AV block Type II, third-degree AV block
set2.q: A 64-year-old woman's cardiologist calls her rhythm Mobitz I. Which block is that?
opts: Second-degree type II (Mobitz II)
Second-degree type II is the one called Mobitz II, with a constant PR interval before the dropped beats.
Second-degree type I
Correct. Second-degree type I is also called Wenckebach, or Mobitz I; second-degree type II is Mobitz II.
Third-degree block
Third-degree block is called complete heart block: no P waves are conducted at all.
First-degree block
First-degree block has no alternative name in this scheme. It is a prolonged PR interval with every P wave conducted.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 22

set2.io: Correlate ECG findings with clinical implications of ventricular arrhythmias and AV blocks
set2.q: A 59-year-old man collapses. No carotid pulse is felt, and the monitor shows this. What is the rhythm?
opts: Normal sinus rhythm
The tracing looks like sinus rhythm, but a rhythm with no pulse is not sinus rhythm. Organized activity without a pulse is pulseless electrical activity.
Ventricular standstill
Ventricular standstill shows P waves with no QRS complexes. Every P wave here is followed by a QRS and a T wave.
Pulseless electrical activity
Correct. Organized electrical activity on the monitor with no mechanical activity, no pulse, is pulseless electrical activity, whatever rhythm it looks like.
Asystole
Asystole has no electrical activity. This monitor shows organized P waves, QRS complexes and T waves.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 16
set2.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block Type I, second-degree AV block Type II, third-degree AV block
set2.q: A 61-year-old man has second-degree type I block. Which describes his P waves?
opts: Absent across the strip
P waves are present in every atrioventricular block; the atria keep firing. Absent P waves point elsewhere.
Unrelated to any QRS complex
P waves unrelated to the QRS complexes are third-degree block. In type I they are conducted until one drops.
Conducted until one is dropped
Correct. In type I the P waves are present, normal and married to the QRS complexes except for the dropped beat.
Conducted after a constant PR
A constant PR on every conducted beat is type II. In type I the PR lengthens.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 30

set2.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of AV nodal and infranodal conduction abnormalities
set2.q: A 77-year-old woman has complete heart block. Which two pacemakers drive her heart?
opts: The sinoatrial node and an escape
Correct. There are two independent pacemakers: the sinoatrial node for the atria, and either the atrioventricular junction or the Purkinje and bundle-branch fibers for the ventricles.
Two foci within the ventricles
Only the ventricular pacemaker is below the block. The atria are still driven by the sinoatrial node.
Two foci within the atria
The atria are driven by the sinoatrial node alone. The ventricles need their own escape pacemaker below the block.
The sinoatrial node alone
The sinoatrial node cannot reach the ventricles through a complete block, so a second pacemaker must take over below it.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 42

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes
set2.q: A 66-year-old woman's monitor shows a regular rhythm with a P wave before each QRS, but she has no pulse. What does this combination represent?
opts: Mechanical activity without electrical activity
Contraction needs depolarization first, so this combination does not occur. The monitor shows electricity; the muscle is not producing a pulse.
Atrial activity without ventricular activity
That is ventricular standstill, with P waves and no QRS. This monitor shows QRS complexes after every P wave.
Electrical activity without mechanical activity
Correct. Pulseless electrical activity is organized electrical activity on the monitor with no mechanical activity, so there is no pulse.
No electrical or mechanical activity
That is asystole, a flat line. This monitor shows organized complexes.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 16

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
set2.q: A 58-year-old woman is told her wide-complex tachycardia arises below the atria. Which statement defines ventricular tachycardia?
opts: A tachycardia from the atrioventricular node
A rhythm from the atrioventricular node is junctional, not ventricular. Ventricular tachycardia starts in the ventricles themselves.
A tachycardia that originates in the ventricles
Correct. Ventricular tachycardia refers to any tachycardia that originates in the ventricles, monomorphic or polymorphic.
Chaotic firing of many ventricular foci
Chaotic firing of multiple foci is ventricular fibrillation, which produces no organized complexes and no cardiac output.
A fast sinus rhythm with a wide QRS
A sinus rhythm keeps a P wave before each QRS. Ventricular tachycardia has no P waves, or dissociated ones, because the ventricles drive it.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 5

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block Type I, second-degree AV block Type II, third-degree AV block
set2.q: A 62-year-old woman's monitor prints this strip. What is the rhythm?
opts: Second-degree type II (Mobitz II)
Type II has a PR that stays the same on every conducted beat. These PR intervals lengthen before the dropped beat.
Second-degree type I (Wenckebach)
Correct. Grouped beats with a progressively lengthening PR interval until a P wave is not conducted, then a reset, are second-degree type I.
Third-degree (complete) block
In third-degree block P waves march through unrelated to the QRS. Here the P waves are married to the QRS except the dropped beat.
First-degree atrioventricular block
First-degree block is a long but fixed PR with no dropped beats. This strip drops a beat.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 34
set2.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes
set2.q: A 68-year-old woman is pulseless. Which finding defines asystole rather than another arrest rhythm?
opts: An organized rhythm with no pulse
Organized activity without a pulse is pulseless electrical activity. Asystole has no electrical activity at all.
P waves with no QRS complexes
Atrial P waves without ventricular complexes are ventricular standstill. Asystole has no P waves either.
Chaotic waves with no QRS
Chaotic waves without measurable complexes are ventricular fibrillation. Asystole has no waves.
No electrical activity at all
Correct. Asystole is a lack of electrical activity, a flat line, with no pulse.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 15

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block, third-degree AV block
set2.q: A 66-year-old woman's PR interval just before a dropped beat is longer than the PR just after it. Which block is this?
opts: Second-degree type II (Mobitz II)
Type II has PR intervals of equal duration before and after the dropped beat, because its PR is constant.
Second-degree type I
Correct. If the PR intervals before and after the dropped beat differ in duration, it is always second-degree type I (Wenckebach).
Third-degree block
Third-degree block has no consistent PR relationship and no single dropped beat; every P wave is unconducted.
First-degree block
First-degree block never drops a beat. Every P wave is conducted after a long PR.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 50

set2.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of AV nodal and infranodal conduction abnormalities
set2.q: A 65-year-old man in ventricular fibrillation has no pulse. Why is there no pulse in this rhythm?
opts: The ventricles quiver, not contract
Correct. Chaotic firing leaves the heart muscle unable to contract, so it quivers; with no ventricular contraction there is no cardiac output and no pulse.
The atria stop firing completely
Atrial activity is not what fails. In ventricular fibrillation the ventricles quiver and never contract, which is why output stops.
The QRS complexes are too wide
There are no measurable QRS complexes in ventricular fibrillation. The pulse is absent because the ventricles do not contract.
The sinoatrial node is blocked
A sinoatrial block would not stop the ventricles quivering. The problem is chaotic ventricular firing with no contraction.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 12

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
set2.q: A 76-year-old woman in cardiac arrest is monitored, and this strip is recorded. What change does it show?
opts: Ventricular tachycardia becoming sinus rhythm
Sinus rhythm would show organized P, QRS and T waves. The right side of this strip is a flat line with no activity.
Asystole becoming ventricular fibrillation
The order is reversed: the strip starts with chaotic waves and ends flat. That is fibrillation becoming asystole.
Torsades becoming ventricular tachycardia
Both of those have large wide complexes. Here small chaotic waves end in a flat line with no complexes at all.
Ventricular fibrillation becoming asystole
Correct. Chaotic fibrillatory waves on the left give way to a flat line on the right: ventricular fibrillation degenerating into asystole.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 15
set2.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block, third-degree AV block
set2.q: An 82-year-old woman has this strip. Which relationship between the P waves and the QRS complexes does it show?
opts: A QRS after each P at a long PR
One QRS per P wave at a long PR is first-degree block. Here the P waves outnumber the QRS complexes.
A PR that lengthens until one drops
Progressive lengthening to a dropped beat is second-degree type I. Here the PR is never consistent.
None: each beats at its own regular rate
Correct. In third-degree block regular P-P intervals are unrelated to regular R-R intervals; atrial and ventricular activity are totally independent.
A constant PR with occasional drops
A constant PR with dropped beats is second-degree type II. Here no PR interval repeats.

set2.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
set2.q: A 73-year-old man is found diaphoretic, and the monitor shows this rhythm. What is it?
opts: Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
The polymorphic form is irregular and its complexes change shape and twist. These complexes are identical from beat to beat.
Coarse ventricular fibrillation
Ventricular fibrillation, coarse or fine, is chaotic, with no measurable QRS. This rhythm is perfectly organized.
Atrial and ventricular pacing
Dual pacing shows a spike before the P wave and another before each QRS. There are no pacer spikes on this strip.
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
Correct. Large, regular complexes of one identical shape with no P waves are monomorphic ventricular tachycardia.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 5
set2.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

set2.io: Correlate ECG findings with clinical implications of ventricular arrhythmias and AV blocks
set2.q: A 55-year-old man has an episode of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that twists around the baseline. Which interval abnormality is it usually a consequence of?
opts: A prolonged PR interval
A long PR interval is first-degree atrioventricular block, a benign conduction delay. It does not produce torsades.
A shortened QT interval
It is a prolonged QT interval, not a short one, that sets up torsades de pointes.
A widened P wave
A wide, notched P wave points to left atrial enlargement. Torsades follows a prolonged QT interval.
A prolonged QT interval
Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia of the torsades type is usually a consequence of a prolonged QT interval.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 11

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
set2.q: A 63-year-old woman's monitor shows this rhythm. Which feature on the strip gives the rhythm its name?
opts: Twisting of the points
Correct. Torsades de pointes is French for twisting of the points: the complexes swing from positive to negative around the baseline.
Identical wide complexes
Identical complexes are the monomorphic form of ventricular tachycardia. Torsades is polymorphic, changing shape as it twists.
P waves without QRS complexes
P waves marching with no QRS complexes are ventricular standstill. This strip is all ventricular activity.
A pacer spike before each QRS
A spike before each wide QRS is a ventricular paced rhythm. There are no pacer spikes here.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 5
set2.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
set2.q: A 55-year-old woman's monitor shows a regular tachycardia with no P waves. Which QRS finding fits ventricular tachycardia?
opts: Narrow
A narrow QRS means the impulse traveled down the normal conduction pathway from above the ventricles. Ventricular tachycardia is wide.
Not measurable
An unmeasurable QRS is ventricular fibrillation, where there are no organized complexes. Ventricular tachycardia has measurable, wide complexes.
Wide
Correct. The QRS in ventricular tachycardia is wide, because the impulse starts in the ventricle and spreads outside the normal conduction pathway.
Absent
No QRS at all is asystole or ventricular standstill. Ventricular tachycardia produces a QRS with every beat, and it is wide.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 6

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
set2.q: A 49-year-old woman collapses on the ward, and this rhythm is on her monitor. What is it?
opts: Torsades de pointes
Correct. An irregular, polymorphic ventricular tachycardia whose complexes swell and shrink as they twist around the baseline is torsades de pointes.
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia is regular, with complexes of one shape. These complexes change shape and amplitude from beat to beat.
Ventricular fibrillation
Ventricular fibrillation is chaotic, with no measurable QRS. This strip still has large ventricular complexes, twisting in a pattern.
Ventricular standstill
Ventricular standstill shows P waves marching across with no QRS at all. This strip is full of rapid ventricular complexes.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 11
set2.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block Type I, second-degree AV block Type II, third-degree AV block
set2.q: A 34-year-old woman feels well. Her PR interval is longer than 0.20 seconds (normal 0.12 to 0.20) on this strip. What is the rhythm?
opts: First-degree atrioventricular block
Correct. A sinus rhythm with every P wave conducted and a PR interval beyond 0.2 seconds is first-degree atrioventricular block.
Second-degree type I (Wenckebach)
Type I shows a PR that lengthens until a P wave is not conducted. On this strip every P wave is followed by a QRS.
Second-degree type II (Mobitz II)
Type II drops QRS complexes after some P waves. Nothing is dropped on this strip.
Third-degree (complete) block
Third-degree block shows P waves unrelated to the QRS. Here each P wave is married to the QRS that follows it.

set2.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

set2.q: A 78-year-old man's monitor shows this. What is his cardiac output?
opts: Normal, because the atria contract
Atrial contraction alone does not pump blood to the body. With no ventricular contraction there is no output.
None, although the atria contract
Correct. This is ventricular standstill: atrial contractions with no ventricular contractions, so there is no detectable pulse and no cardiac output.
Reduced, from a slow escape rhythm
A slow escape rhythm would show QRS complexes. There are none here, so there is no ventricular output.
Normal if the P waves are regular
Regular P waves show only that the atria are firing. The ventricles are not contracting, so there is no output.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 17
set2.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block Type I, second-degree AV block Type II, third-degree AV block
set2.q: A 56-year-old man has intermittent dizziness, and this strip is recorded. What is the rhythm?
opts: Second-degree type I (Wenckebach)
Correct. The PR interval lengthens beat to beat until a P wave is not conducted and a QRS drops, then the cycle starts over: Wenckebach.
Second-degree type II (Mobitz II)
Type II keeps a constant PR interval before the dropped beat. Here each PR is longer than the one before.
First-degree atrioventricular block
First-degree block never drops a QRS. This strip has a P wave with no QRS after it.
Third-degree (complete) block
Third-degree block has no PR relationship at all. Here the PR follows a predictable lengthening pattern.

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
set2.q: A 69-year-old woman collapses in the waiting room and has no pulse. Her monitor shows this. What is the rhythm?
opts: Ventricular fibrillation
Correct. Irregular, chaotic waves with no measurable P waves, QRS complexes or T waves are ventricular fibrillation.
Torsades de pointes
Torsades has large wide complexes that twist in amplitude around the baseline. This strip has no organized complexes at all.
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia is regular, with identical wide complexes. These waves vary in size and shape with no pattern.
Asystole
Asystole is a flat line, a lack of electrical activity. This strip shows continuous chaotic electrical activity.

set2.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of AV nodal and infranodal conduction abnormalities
set2.q: A 69-year-old man is told he has an atrioventricular heart block. What does that term describe?
opts: Chaotic firing of ventricular foci
Chaotic firing of many ventricular foci is ventricular fibrillation. A heart block is a conduction delay or failure between atria and ventricles.
Failure of the sinoatrial node to fire
In the heart blocks the atria keep firing; P waves are present. The problem is getting the atrial impulse through to the ventricles.
A rapid rhythm from the ventricles
A rapid ventricular rhythm is ventricular tachycardia. A heart block is about conduction from the atria to the ventricles.
Delayed or failed atrioventricular conduction
Correct. Atrioventricular junction blocks are a delay in, or a complete failure of, the conduction of an atrial impulse through the atrioventricular node.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 22

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
set2.q: A 74-year-old woman with a pacemaker has this strip. Which pacing does it show?
opts: Ventricular pacing
Ventricular pacing puts the spike right before a wide QRS with an opposite-direction T wave. These QRS complexes are narrow and normal.
Atrial and ventricular pacing
Dual pacing shows two spikes per beat, one before the P wave and one before the QRS. This strip shows one spike per beat.
No pacing, sinus rhythm
Each cycle here starts with a pacer spike, so the pacemaker, not the sinoatrial node, is firing.
Atrial pacing
Correct. A pacer spike followed by a normal P-QRS-T cycle is an atrial paced rhythm: the pacemaker takes over for the sinoatrial node.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 19
set2.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block, third-degree AV block
set2.q: A 39-year-old man has first-degree atrioventricular block. How many of his P waves are conducted to the ventricles?
opts: None of them
No conducted P waves is third-degree block. First-degree block conducts every one, slowly.
All of them
Correct. In first-degree block the P waves are all conducted on the tracing; conduction is only delayed, not interrupted.
All but the last in each group
Grouped beats ending in a non-conducted P wave are second-degree type I. First-degree block drops none.
Most, with some dropped
Dropped P waves define second-degree block. First-degree block conducts all of them.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 23

set2.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of AV nodal and infranodal conduction abnormalities
set2.q: A 76-year-old woman with an atrial pacemaker has a normal-looking QRS after each spike. Why is her QRS normal?
opts: It paces the ventricles directly
Pacing the ventricles directly gives a wide QRS. An atrial pacemaker fires in the atria and lets the normal pathway carry the beat.
It bypasses the atrioventricular node
An atrial pacemaker relies on the atrioventricular node and the rest of the pathway. It does not bypass them.
It uses the intact normal conduction pathway
Correct. Atrial pacemakers take over for the sinoatrial node and depend on an intact, properly functioning conduction pathway, so the QRS is normal.
It fires only after each QRS
The spike comes before the cycle, followed by a normal P-QRS-T. It starts the beat rather than following it.
set2.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 18

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block, third-degree AV block
set2.q: A 70-year-old man has second-degree type II block. Which statement about his dropped beats is correct?
opts: Only one ever drops at a time
Type II can drop more than one beat in a row; that is part of why it is the more serious second-degree block.
Beats drop after the PR lengthens
Dropping after progressive PR lengthening is second-degree type I. In type II the PR stays constant.
More than one may drop in a row
Correct. In second-degree type II it is possible to have more than one dropped beat in a row.
No beats drop; only the PR is long
A long PR with no dropped beats is first-degree block. Type II drops QRS complexes.
